topics.topic: Data-directory privacy, allowed object types, and continued integrity enforcement
questions: What exact ownership and mode conditions mean `private`, which nested entries are checked, and must those conditions continue to be enforced after startup and on every newly created file?
Are hard links, FIFOs, sockets, devices and unexpected regular files or directories permitted anywhere in the data directory, and what must startup or a later store call do on finding them?
What exact ownership, mode, ACL, hard-link and object-type conditions make the directory and each contained object "private"?
Are ownership and permission checks repeated on later store calls as the symlink check is, and what happens if an object becomes non-private after startup?
What exact ownership, permission bits, ACLs, special-file types and hard-link conditions satisfy “private,” and are they checked only at startup or again on use?

What happens when a managed object encountered later is missing, has changed owner or permissions, is the wrong non-symlink type, has unexpected hard links, or its recorded bytes fail digest or size checks?

quotes: The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise.
judgement.why: The topic concerns A18's unchanged data-directory privacy rule, and the Linux/O_NOFOLLOW change to A17 and A20 did not make that existing question matter.

topics.topic: Event defining serialized arrival order for concurrent requests
questions: What defines arrival order when two requests are received concurrently or become readable together, and is that order required to be reproducible or externally observable?
What event establishes arrival order when requests overlap: connection acceptance, first byte, complete message receipt, schema-valid dispatch, or entry into a serialized queue?

What observable event defines arrival order when concurrent MCP requests are received: complete message receipt, transport acceptance, authentication completion, or insertion into an explicit sequence?

quotes:
Surface requests are handled one at a time in the order they arrive: one request, including the run
   advancement it causes (A13), ends before the next begins, so an approval, a
   cancellation and a resume of one run never race.
judgement.why: The serialization sentence is unchanged, and the reopening change did not affect concurrent-request ordering.

topics.topic: Filesystem publication, SQLite commit ordering, flushing, and crash durability
questions: What does `flushed` require, where must the temporary file reside, when are the containing directory and SQLite transaction made durable, and what crash states are permitted between rename and database commit?

What durability and ordering guarantee must hold across the SQLite commit and publication of one or several files if the process or host crashes, especially whether a committed record may ever name a missing or incomplete file?
Does "flushed" require an OS durability operation on the file and containing directory, and when may a successful store call be acknowledged relative to SQLite and filesystem synchronization?
What ordering and durability operations guarantee that a committed database record never names a missing, incomplete or uncommitted file after a crash?

quotes:
Value bytes and spooled files are written to a temporary file, flushed, checked
   against their digest and size, and then renamed into place; a completed file a record names is
   never overwritten — a spooled file no record names, left by a change that
   failed, is replaced at its position.
judgement.why: The topic concerns unchanged A18 publication and durability language, which the reopening change did not affect.

topics.topic: Provisioning and handling of a partially existing data-directory layout
questions: Must the data directory and its layout already exist, or may the kernel create the directory, database, value areas and spool areas; and what happens when only part of the layout exists?
Must the data directory, SQLite database, value area and spool already exist, or does the kernel create any missing part; and what happens when only some of them exist?
Must the data directory, database, value area, fixture area and spool already exist, or does the kernel create any missing part, and with what behavior for a partially existing layout?

quotes:
The data directory holds one SQLite database with every kernel record, a
   content-addressed area of value bytes and file fixtures named by digest, and
   the run spool, one subdirectory per run.
judgement.why: The required layout passage is unchanged, and the Linux/O_NOFOLLOW change did not make provisioning behavior newly material.

topics.topic: Secure component opening and behavior when O_NOFOLLOW is unavailable
questions: Which access flags and type checks apply to intermediate path components, and therefore which directory permissions and non-directory components cause refusal?
What must happen if the Python/runtime interface or the mounted filesystem does not support `O_NOFOLLOW`, despite the host identifying as Linux?
What must happen if the Linux/Python runtime does not expose or honor `O_NOFOLLOW`, given that the kernel must use it but is forbidden to test for its presence?
Which other flags and component types are permitted when opening intermediate components, and what happens when the host or filesystem rejects `O_NOFOLLOW`?

quotes:
Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without
   following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's
   `O_NOFOLLOW`, whose presence no code tests (A20 rule 3), and the checks and the read use
   that one opened file, so the file checked is the file read.

A release runs on Linux and
   on no other host, no version named (owner, 2026-10-18).
judgement.divergence: One implementer can use directory-only descriptor opens and refuse an unreadable or non-directory intermediate component or any filesystem rejection of `O_NOFOLLOW`; another can use a different Linux open mode or a race-resistant fallback and accept the same configured path. The installer notices whether the kernel starts and which paths it accepts.
judgement.why: The new rule mandates `O_NOFOLLOW` but leaves the other component-opening conditions and rejection behavior open.

topics.topic: Startup behavior when temporary or unreferenced-object cleanup fails
questions: Does failure to remove a temporary file or unreferenced value byte also allow startup to continue, as explicitly stated only for spool directories, or does it stop startup?
Does failure to enumerate or remove a temporary file or unreferenced value byte stop startup, get ignored like an unremovable obsolete spool directory, or leave the object quarantined?
Does failure to enumerate or remove a temporary file or unreferenced value stop startup, as opposed to the explicitly tolerated failure to remove an obsolete spool directory?

quotes:
On start, temporary files,
   value bytes no record names (left by a failed call, K-10; owner,
   2026-10-07) and
   the spool directories of runs that ended and do not keep their spool (A14) are
   removed; nothing else is. A spool directory that cannot be removed does not
   stop the start: it stays, never served, until a later start removes it.
judgement.why: The cleanup passage is unchanged, and the reopening change did not affect cleanup failures.

topics.topic: Startup handling of absent, corrupt, inconsistent, or incompatible stores
questions: What must startup do when the database is absent, malformed, corrupt, locked by an unrelated process, has an unsupported schema, or cannot provide the durability and transaction behavior the rules assume?
How does a release recognize the database schema and filesystem-layout version, and what must it do with a store created by an older, newer or incompatible release?
What must startup do when the SQLite database is malformed or inconsistent, or a record names a missing, truncated or digest-mismatched durable value or trial fixture?

quotes:
The data directory holds one SQLite database with every kernel record, a
   content-addressed area of value bytes and file fixtures named by digest, and
   the run spool, one subdirectory per run.
judgement.why: Store corruption and compatibility concern an unchanged A18 passage and were not made material by the Linux/O_NOFOLLOW change.

topics.topic: Supported Linux platform and filesystem capability baseline
questions: Without a Linux version or capability baseline, which kernel, libc, CPU architecture and filesystem implementations are supported, and what happens when Linux lacks semantics required by namespaces, `O_NOFOLLOW`, resource limits, locking, SQLite or atomic durable rename?

What exactly counts as a supported Linux host—kernel/ABI floor, CPU architecture, libc, distribution, containers, WSL or Android—and is compatibility with every such host promised or only with hosts satisfying unstated prerequisites?

Which Linux kernel capabilities or minimum version, CPU architectures, userspace ABI and libc environments are supported, and is an otherwise unsupported Linux host rejected by a check or merely outside the release guarantee?

Does every Linux filesystem qualify even when it cannot provide the exclusive locking, atomic rename, directory durability or SQLite locking semantics A18 requires, or must the release restrict or probe the data-directory filesystem?

quotes:
A release runs on Linux and
   on no other host, no version named (owner, 2026-10-18).
judgement.divergence: One implementer can treat every Linux environment as supported until an operation fails, while another can reject Linux hosts lacking selected namespace, locking, rename, resource-limit, SQLite or filesystem capabilities at startup. The installer notices whether the release is supported and whether the kernel starts.
judgement.why: The new Linux-only rule states no capability baseline or behavior for Linux systems that lack semantics the other rules require.

topics.topic: Atomic transaction boundaries for multi-record and multi-file changes
questions: Which groups of record and file changes constitute one `change` and therefore one atomic store call, especially for admission, activation, run advancement, cancellation, release and startup cleanup where the other rules describe multiple related writes?

Which records and file publications constitute one “change” for each multi-record action, and therefore must commit atomically—for example run creation, admission plus activation, refusal plus run termination, and a node outcome plus produced values?

quotes:
Every change is one call to the
   store module and one transaction inside it; callers never open, name or pass a
   transaction (K-17).
judgement.why: The meaning of a store change is an unchanged A18 question unaffected by the reopening change.

topics.topic: Configured-path syntax, normalization, and relative-path resolution
questions: Must the configuration path be absolute, or are relative paths, `.` and `..` components accepted, and from which directory is a relative path resolved?
How are `.` and `..` components, repeated separators, and a trailing separator in an absolute configured path handled: literally, normalized before opening, or refused?

quotes:
The kernel reads the file's path from its one command-line argument and reads
   no environment variable.

Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without
   following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's
   `O_NOFOLLOW`, whose presence no code tests (A20 rule 3), and the checks and the read use
   that one opened file, so the file checked is the file read.
judgement.divergence: One implementer can reject relative paths and `.` or `..` components; another can resolve them against the process working directory or normalize them before component traversal. The installer notices whether startup accepts the argument and which configuration file is loaded.
judgement.why: The component-opening rule does not define the configured path grammar or relative-path resolution, producing observable startup behavior.

topics.topic: Definition and enforcement of the Linux-only host boundary
questions: What exactly qualifies a host as Linux, and how and when must the kernel refuse to run on a non-Linux or compatibility-layer host?
Is non-Linux exclusion enforced by packaging/build selection or by a kernel startup check, and if a binary is executed on an unsupported host, what observable failure and check precedence apply?

quotes:
The owner decided on 2026-10-18: the kernel runs only on Linux, no
    version named; another host is unsupported.

A20 rule 3 (`02_rules_installation.md`) says so; its formal invariants
      gain `host = linux`. Rule 3 stays outside the running kernel (State 3).
judgement.why: State 6 decides that non-Linux hosts are unsupported and that the host rule is not enforced by a running-kernel check.

topics.topic: Exclusive-lock object, primitive, lifetime, and failure handling
questions: What object and Linux locking primitive define the exclusive lock, how long is it held, and how are missing, stale, malformed or otherwise unopenable lock objects classified?
What object and locking semantics define this lock, and how are a stale lock file, an unsupported lock operation, or another lock-acquisition error handled?

quotes:
At start it takes an exclusive lock in the data
   directory; a second process on the same directory refuses to start.
judgement.why: The lock requirement is unchanged, and the reopening change did not affect its object, primitive or lifetime.

topics.topic: Symlink-safe component traversal and protection against path-replacement races
questions: Does the no-follow requirement apply component by component to directories as well as to the final file, and how must the implementation prevent a directory from being replaced by a symlink between the startup scan and a later open?
Does A18 require component-by-component descriptor-relative traversal with `O_NOFOLLOW`, as the changed A17 now explicitly requires, or only a no-follow check on the final file?

quotes:
Every
   file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link
   found at start stops the start, and one found later makes that store call
   fail with nothing written.
judgement.why: A18's store traversal requirement is unchanged; making A17's separate configuration traversal more explicit did not alter the store rule.

topics.topic: Validation and handling of existing content at a digest path
questions: What happens when the target digest path already exists but its bytes, size or expected type do not match the bytes being published, whether because of corruption or a SHA-256 collision?
When a digest path already exists, must the kernel verify its type, size and digest before reuse, and what happens if the existing bytes do not match?

quotes:
Equal bytes are stored once. On start, temporary files,
   value bytes no record names (left by a failed call, K-10; owner,
   2026-10-07) and
   the spool directories of runs that ended and do not keep their spool (A14) are
   removed; nothing else is.
judgement.why: Existing content at a digest path concerns unchanged A18 storage language and was not affected by the reopening change.

topics.topic: Assignment and ordering of immutable store positions
questions: What event assigns a record's immutable store position, whether updates to mutable entities receive new positions, and how positions are ordered when one transaction creates several records?

topics.topic: Data-directory path identity, aliases, mounts, and symlink allowance
questions: What counts as the same directory when configured paths use symbolic links, bind mounts, different textual paths or filesystem aliases, and is the data-directory path itself allowed to be a symbolic link?

topics.topic: Ordering and failure precedence of startup checks
questions: In what exact order are the lock, directory ownership and permission checks, symlink scan, database validation, cleanup, A17 configuration checks and A03 sandbox probe performed, and which failure is reported when several fail?

topics.topic: Whether failed store calls may leave unreferenced published files
questions: Does “nothing written” prohibit even a published but unreferenced file, or does A18 rule 3's allowance that a failed call may leave “a published file no record names” also apply when the failure is a later symlink?
